title: Looking ahead
goals: Make confident predictions about the future with will and won't.
Talk about possibilities with may, might and expressions like maybe and probably.
Use the simple present with if, when, after and before to talk about the future.
Offer help and make promises with I'll and I won't, and accept requests with All right / OK.
Talk about work, life plans and jobs.
Write about the future, ordering your ideas with First, Second, Next and Finally.

learn.title: will and won't: confident predictions
learn.html:
We use will for facts and predictions about the future that we are very sure about. It is the same for all persons: no -s, and it is followed by the base verb (without to).

FormExample
Positive: will / 'll + verbI'll be 30 in June. The baby will keep us busy.
Negative: won't (= will not) + verbIt won't be easy to find a job.
Question: Will + subject + verb?Will you travel next year? — Yes, I will. / No, I won't.
  • will = prediction or future fact; for plans already decided use be going to or the present continuous: I'm going to Europe next year.
  • For predictions with visible evidence, use be going to: Look at those clouds. It's going to rain.
  • With I think, I guess, maybe, probably you can use will even if you are not 100% sure: We'll probably take some time off.

watch.wrong: I will to call you tomorrow.
watch.why: After will, use the base verb, without to.

watch.wrong: She will goes to the party.
watch.right: She will go to the party.
watch.why: Will doesn't change and the verb after it has no -s.

watch.wrong: I will go to Cancún next week; I already bought the tickets.
watch.right: I'm going to Cancún next week; I already bought the tickets.
watch.why: For plans already decided, use be going to or the present continuous, not will.

learn.title: may and might: when you're not sure
learn.html:
We use may or might when something is possible but not certain. In this use they mean almost the same thing ("maybe", "it could be").

FormExample
Positive: may / might + verbI may go on for a master's degree.
Negative: may / might + not + verbI might not be able to afford it.
With will + a doubt wordWe'll probably take some time off. Maybe we'll move.
  • Don't use can to predict when you're not sure: It may rain (not It can rain).
  • may / might don't take to or -s: She might leave.
  • mayn't and mightn't are not used in everyday English; say may not / might not.
  • Maybe (one word) goes at the beginning: Maybe I'll study abroad. May be (two words) is the verb: It may be true.

watch.wrong: He can come to the party, but I'm not sure.
watch.right: He might come to the party, but I'm not sure.
watch.why: For an uncertain possibility use may / might, not can.

watch.wrong: I might to travel around Europe.
May be I'll move to Monterrey.
watch.why: At the start of a sentence write maybe, as one word.

learn.title: Simple present with future meaning: if, when, after, before
learn.html:
In sentences with two parts about the future, the part that begins with if, when, after or before goes in the simple present, even when you are talking about the future. The other part uses will, may, might or be going to.

ConnectorExample
ifIf I get good grades, I may go to law school.
whenWhat are you going to do when you graduate?
afterAfter I graduate, I'll be able to work in my parents' firm.
beforeI need to decide before I go home for the summer.
  • If the part with if / when comes first, put a comma: When I graduate, I'll look for a job. If it comes at the end, no comma: I'll look for a job when I graduate.
  • English uses the simple present here, where Spanish often uses the subjunctive: when I graduate.

watch.wrong: When I will graduate, I'll look for a job.
watch.right: When I graduate, I'll look for a job.
watch.why: After when, don't use will: simple present.

watch.wrong: If you will study, you'll pass.
watch.why: After if, use the simple present.

watch.wrong: After I will finish, I'll call you.
watch.right: After I finish, I'll call you.
watch.why: After after, use the simple present.

watch.wrong: I'll call you when I will arrive.
watch.right: I'll call you when I arrive.
watch.why: The when clause uses the simple present even when it refers to the future.

learn.title: Offers and promises with I'll and I won't
learn.html:
With I'll we offer help in the moment; with I will / I won't we promise something.

FunctionExample
Offer: I'll + verbI'll get some steaks. I'll drive.
Promise: I'll / I won't + verbI'll call you. I won't forget the drinks.
Short answer to a promiseA: Make sure you buy gas. B: All right. I will.
Accepting a requestA: Remind me to bring my umbrella. B: All right. / OK.
  • The short answer to a promise uses full will, without a contraction: I will. (not I'll.)
  • remind (someone) to + verb: Remind me to call Mom.

watch.wrong: I don't forget your birthday, I promise.
watch.right: I won't forget your birthday, I promise.
watch.why: Promises about the future use will / won't.

watch.wrong: A: Please call me. B: Yes, I'll.
watch.right: A: Please call me. B: Yes, I will.
watch.why: A positive short answer is not contracted.

learn.title: Useful expressions
learn.html:
• I'll be 30 in June. / It won't be easy. — safe predictions.
  • I may / might go on for a master's degree. — possibility.
  • Maybe we'll move. / We'll probably take some time off. — predictions with doubt.
  • I'll drive. / I'll get some steaks. — offering help.
  • I'll call you. / I won't forget. — promising. Reply: All right. I will.
  • All right. / OK. — accepting a request.
  • First, ... Second, ... Next, ... Finally, ... — ordering ideas when writing: First, you won't need to drive. Second, you'll never get lost.

write.prompt: Write a text of 120 to 180 words about your plans for the next five years: work, studies and personal life. Use will / won't for what you think is certain, may / might for what is possible, and at least three sentences with if, when, after or before. Opening: In five years, I'll probably...
targets: if / when / after / before + simple present
checklist: Two predictions with will or won't
Two possibilities with may or might
Three sentences with if, when, after or before + simple present
No will after if / when / after / before
Work or plans vocabulary (retire, get a degree, study abroad...)
write.model:
In five years, I'll probably be a manager in my company. I'm studying at night now, so I think I'll get a degree in business next year. After I finish my studies, I will look for a better job. I won't stay in the same position forever, because I want to learn new things.

I may change cities, and I might study abroad for one year. If I save enough money, I'll travel to Canada. When I live there, I will improve my English a lot. I might also learn a little French, but I'm not sure.

In my personal life, I will probably get married and buy a small house. I won't have children before I'm thirty-two, I think. Before I buy a house, I will talk to a bank about a loan. If everything goes well, my parents will visit me every summer. I hope I'll be healthy and happy. When I retire, many years later, I'll relax in a small town by the sea, and I won't need to wake up early every day.

write.prompt: Write an article of 120 to 180 words titled Life in 2050: how life and work will be. Organize your ideas with First, Second, Next and Finally, and use will, won't and might. Opening: First, people won't need to...
checklist: The four connectors First, Second, Next, Finally at the start of ideas
Three predictions with will or won't
One possibility with might or may
Base verb after will / won't / might
write.model:
Life in 2050

First, people won't need to go to an office every day. Most workers will do their jobs from home, and they will have meetings with 3D holograms. Some companies might even have a four-day work week.

Second, transportation will be very different. Cars will drive themselves, and there won't be many accidents. Cities will be cleaner, because most vehicles will use electricity. I think trains will be faster than planes, and we might travel to other countries in two hours.

Next, jobs will change. Robots will do boring and dangerous work, so factories won't need many people. However, there will still be jobs for plumbers, nurses and teachers because machines can't care for people like humans can. A journalist will use computers to write reports, but he will check the facts himself. New jobs may appear that we can't imagine today.

Finally, I think people will live longer and healthier lives. Doctors will cure many diseases, and we might live to be one hundred years old. It will be an exciting world.

reading.title: Four Friends, Four Futures
reading.intro: Read the article about four friends who finish university and answer.
paragraphs: Next June, four friends from Monterrey will graduate from college. They are excited, but they are also a little nervous. What will they do after graduation? We asked each of them about their plans.

Ana studied architecture. She says she'll find a job right away. "I'm sure it won't be easy, but I'll work hard," she says. "My uncle has a design company. If he has a place for me, I'll start there in July. Maybe I'll find my own place in a year or two. Before that, I need to save some money." She also might go on for a master's degree, but only if she gets a scholarship.

Luis is the family's future doctor, but he won't start his career soon. "When I finish college, I'm going to study for six more years," he explains. "It'll be a long road. After I graduate, I'll take some time off. I'm going to travel around Europe with my brother for a month. We'll probably visit Italy and Spain." Luis thinks he may study abroad, but he's not sure yet.

Marta wants to be a journalist. "I'll look for a job at a newspaper," she says. "If I get good grades, I might get an interview with a big magazine. I think I'll earn less money than my friends, but I'll have a very rewarding job." Marta also has a surprise: she's going to have a baby in October! "The baby will keep us busy, but my husband and I are very happy," she says.

Finally, there's Diego. He is the only one who doesn't know what to do. "I may work for my father's company, or I might become a firefighter. I really don't know. Maybe I'll decide after I come back from my vacation. Before I make a decision, I'll talk to my friends." His friends laughed and said, "We'll help you, Diego. We promise!"
Four friends, four different futures. What will happen? Only time will tell.

listening.title: Planning a beach trip
listening.intro: Listen to two friends planning a trip to the beach. You can repeat the conversation.

lines.text: OK, Tom. The trip to the beach is on Saturday. What do we need?
Let's see. I'll drive, because my car is bigger. And I'll bring the GPS.
Great. I'll make the sandwiches. Maybe I'll also bring some fruit.
Good idea. Please remind me to buy gas on Friday. Last time we almost ran out of gas!
All right. I will. And you have to leave early. If we leave at seven, we'll miss the traffic.
OK. I'll pick you up at seven. I won't be late, I promise.
Thanks. What about the beach umbrella? It'll be very sunny.
Oh, I might forget it. Remind me to bring it.
Sure. I'll send you a message on Friday night. Also, after we get there, we'll probably have lunch first.
Sounds good. When we finish lunch, we may go swimming.
And if it rains, we'll go to the museum in town.
Perfect. I'm sure it won't rain, though. See you Saturday!
